text: From 35 degrees north, the outer edge of a Saturn-proportioned Earth ring would peak roughly 33 degrees above the horizon, about a third of the way to the zenith (geometric calculation).
as_written: At its highest it climbs about a third of the way up the sky
source: Geometric calculation using Saturn ring radii from NASA/JPL Cassini and Earth's equatorial radius from the NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Saturn's main rings are more than 95 percent water ice.
as_written: more than 95 percent water ice
source: NASA/JPL Cassini mission; Cuzzi et al. 2010, Science, Saturn's rings review

text: Ring particles range from dust-sized grains to house-sized boulders.
as_written: from grains of dust to boulders as big as houses
source: NASA/JPL Cassini mission ring science pages

text: Saturn's main rings are often only about 10 metres thick.
as_written: often only about 10 metres thick
source: NASA/JPL Cassini mission ring science pages

text: The rings are far thinner relative to their width than paper (about 10 m over roughly 62,000 km, versus roughly 0.1 mm over tens of centimetres for paper).
as_written: far thinner, relative to its width, than a sheet of paper
source: Calculation from NASA/JPL ring thickness and ring radii (C ring inner edge 74,658 km to A ring outer edge 136,775 km)

text: Cassini's final orbits in 2017 flew between the rings and the planet and were used to measure ring mass.
as_written: Cassini answered the question in 2017
source: NASA/JPL Cassini Grand Finale; Iess et al. 2019, Science

text: Saturn's ring mass was measured at about 1.5 times 10 to the 19 kilograms, which is 15 billion billion kilograms.
as_written: about 15 billion billion kilograms
source: Iess et al. 2019, Science, Measurement and implications of Saturn's gravity field and ring mass

text: The result was published in 2019.
as_written: published in 2019
source: Iess et al. 2019, Science

text: The ring mass is roughly 40 percent of the mass of Mimas.
as_written: roughly 40 percent of the mass of Saturn's small moon Mimas
source: Iess et al. 2019, Science (about 0.41 Mimas masses)

text: The Moon's mass, about 7.35 times 10 to the 22 kg, is about 4,800 times the ring mass.
as_written: about 4,800 times more
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet compared with Iess et al. 2019

text: Earth's mass, about 5.97 times 10 to the 24 kg, is close to 400,000 times the ring mass.
as_written: close to 400,000 times
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet compared with Iess et al. 2019

text: Saturn's equatorial radius is about 60,000 km (60,268 km).
as_written: about 60,000 kilometres from its centre
source: NASA Saturn Fact Sheet

text: Earth's equatorial radius is about 6,400 km (6,378 km).
as_written: Earth's sits about 6,400
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Saturn's C ring begins at about 74,658 km, which is more than 11 Earth radii.
as_written: more than 11 Earth radii out
source: NASA/JPL Saturn ring dimensions; NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: The Roche limit for icy rubble around Earth falls between roughly 2 and 4.5 Earth radii.
as_written: between about 2 and 4.5 Earth radii
source: Standard Roche limit formulas (rigid and fluid bodies) with Earth mean density 5.51 g/cm3 from NASA Earth Fact Sheet and ice density about 0.92 g/cm3

text: Saturn's main rings run from about 1.24 to 2.27 Saturn radii (C ring inner edge to A ring outer edge).
as_written: from 1.24 to 2.27 times the planet's radius
source: NASA/JPL Saturn ring dimensions (74,658 km to 136,775 km) divided by 60,268 km

text: Scaled to Earth, the ring spans about 1,500 km to 8,100 km altitude and is about 6,600 km wide.
as_written: about 1,500 kilometres above the surface and ends about 8,100 kilometres up
source: Calculation scaling Saturn ring radii by Earth's radius of 6,378 km

text: Scaled ring width is about 6,600 km.
as_written: It is about 6,600 kilometres wide
source: Calculation scaling Saturn ring radii by Earth's radius

text: Keeping the same opacity, a ring scaled to Earth has about 90 times less area and needs about one hundredth of the material.
as_written: Its area is about 90 times smaller
source: Calculation: ratio of Saturn to Earth equatorial radius squared is about 89

text: Removing that mass from the oceans would lower sea level by about half a metre.
as_written: sea level drops by about half a metre
source: Calculation: about 1.7 times 10 to the 17 kg of water over an ocean area of about 361 million square kilometres (NOAA)

text: The Antarctic ice sheet holds ice equivalent to about 58 metres of sea level rise.
as_written: enough to raise the sea by about 58 metres
source: Fretwell et al. 2013, Bedmap2, The Cryosphere; IPCC AR6

text: The ring material needed is under 1 percent of Antarctic ice.
as_written: you have used less than 1 percent
source: Calculation from the half-metre sea level equivalent and 58 metres for Antarctica

text: The Cassini Division is close to 5,000 km wide and is maintained in part by an orbital resonance with Mimas.
as_written: close to 5,000 kilometres wide, and Mimas helps hold it open through an orbital resonance
source: NASA/JPL Cassini mission, Cassini Division (about 4,700 to 4,800 km wide)

text: Scaled to Earth, the Cassini Division would be about 500 km wide.
as_written: about 500 kilometres wide
source: Calculation: roughly 4,700 km times the Earth to Saturn radius ratio of about 0.106

text: The Moon is more than 25 times farther out than the ring's outer edge (about 384,400 km versus about 14,500 km from Earth's centre).
as_written: more than 25 times farther out than the ring's outer edge
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet; calculation from scaled ring radius

text: Circular orbital speed at the inner edge is about 7 km/s and at the outer edge about 5 km/s.
as_written: about 7 kilometres per second. At the outer edge, about 5
source: Calculation from Earth's gravitational parameter GM of 3.986 times 10 to the 14 cubic metres per second squared

text: North of about 64 degrees latitude, the ring's outer edge stays below the horizon.
as_written: North of about 64 degrees
source: Geometric calculation: the ring is visible only where cosine of latitude exceeds the reciprocal of the ring radius in Earth radii

text: The Moon reflects about 12 percent of the light that strikes it.
as_written: about 12 percent of the light that hits it
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet, geometric albedo 0.12

text: Clean water ice reflects substantially more light than lunar rock.
as_written: Clean water ice reflects several times more
source: NASA/JPL Cassini ring photometry

text: Saturn is well over a billion kilometres from Earth.
as_written: from well over a billion kilometres away
source: NASA Saturn Fact Sheet (closest approach to Earth about 1.2 billion km)

text: Earth's axial tilt is 23.4 degrees, so the June Sun is that far north of the equatorial plane.
as_written: the Sun is 23.4 degrees north of that plane
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Earth's shadow is roughly as wide as Earth at ring distances.
as_written: roughly as wide as the planet itself
source: Geometry of the Sun's angular size of about 0.53 degrees over distances of about 10,000 km

text: The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km.
as_written: at about 400 kilometres
source: NASA International Space Station facts

text: GPS satellites orbit at about 20,200 km.
as_written: orbit at about 20,200 kilometres
source: GPS.gov, U.S. Space Force

text: Geostationary orbit is at 35,786 km altitude.
as_written: 35,786 kilometres
source: NASA and ESA reference values for geostationary orbit

text: One gram at 5 km/s carries 12,500 joules (half mass times speed squared), about three grams of TNT at 4.184 kilojoules per gram.
as_written: delivers about 12,500 joules, roughly the energy of three grams of TNT
source: Calculation using kinetic energy and the standard TNT equivalent of 4.184 kJ per gram

text: Pioneer 11 was the first spacecraft to cross Saturn's ring plane, in 1979.
as_written: In 1979, Pioneer 11 became the first spacecraft to cross the plane of Saturn's rings
source: NASA Ames Pioneer 11 mission history

text: Cassini made 22 dives between the rings and Saturn in 2017.
as_written: Cassini dived between the rings and the planet 22 times
source: NASA/JPL Cassini Grand Finale

text: Molniya orbits are inclined at about 63 degrees (63.4 degrees, the critical inclination).
as_written: tilted at about 63 degrees
source: ESA and NASA references on Molniya orbits

text: A Molniya orbit crosses the equatorial plane at about 12,000 km from Earth's centre, within the ring's 7,900 to 14,500 km span.
as_written: about 12,000 kilometres from the centre of the Earth
source: Calculation from Molniya orbital elements (semi-major axis about 26,560 km, eccentricity about 0.74, argument of perigee 270 degrees)

text: Standard geostationary transfer orbits have apsides near the equatorial plane, so they cross it at perigee and apogee.
as_written: crosses the equatorial plane at its lowest point and its highest point
source: Standard geostationary transfer orbit design, ESA and NASA mission design references

text: At the June solstice, noon Sun is behind the ring for latitudes about 6 to 41 degrees south.
as_written: from about 6 degrees south to about 41 degrees south
source: Geometric calculation using Saturn-proportioned ring radii of 1.24 to 2.27 Earth radii and solar declination of 23.4 degrees

text: The city latitudes lie in that belt: Johannesburg about 26 S, Sydney about 34 S, Cape Town about 34 S, Buenos Aires about 35 S, Santiago about 33 S.
as_written: Johannesburg, Sydney, Cape Town, Buenos Aires and Santiago
source: USGS/GeoNames city coordinates compared with the calculated shade belt

text: The B ring (1.53 to 1.95 Saturn radii) would shade about 14 to 27 degrees south at noon at the June solstice, and it is nearly opaque.
as_written: from roughly 14 to 27 degrees south
source: Geometric calculation using NASA/JPL B ring radii (92,000 to 117,580 km); ring opacity from Cassini occultation measurements

text: The inner Van Allen belt spans roughly 1,000 to 6,000 km altitude.
as_written: from about 1,000 to about 6,000 kilometres
source: NASA Van Allen Probes mission

text: Pioneer 11 in 1979 found that Saturn's rings and moons absorb trapped radiation particles; its instrument came from James Van Allen's team.
as_written: it found that Saturn's rings and moons soak up trapped particles
source: Van Allen et al. 1980, Science, Saturn's magnetosphere, rings, and inner satellites

text: Earth passed through Saturn's ring plane in March 2025, making the rings appear to vanish.
as_written: In March 2025, observers on Earth watched its rings seem to vanish
source: NASA and ESA reports on the 2025 Saturn ring-plane crossing

text: Cassini imaged the unlit side of the rings, where dense rings look dark and sparse ones glow.
as_written: The densest ring turns dark. The thin, translucent parts glow
source: NASA/JPL Cassini unlit-side ring imaging

text: Cairo and Houston lie at about 30 degrees north, inside the shaded latitude band.
as_written: over places like Cairo and Houston
source: USGS/GeoNames city coordinates compared with the calculated shade belt

text: Saturn's ring rain drains between 432 and 2,870 kg of water per second, measured with the Keck telescope.
as_written: between 432 and 2,870 kilograms of water every second
source: O'Donoghue et al. 2019, Icarus, Observations of the chemical and thermal response of ring rain on Saturn's ionosphere

text: A 2023 analysis of Cassini dust data argued the rings are no older than a few hundred million years.
as_written: cannot be older than a few hundred million years
source: Kempf et al. 2023, Science Advances, Micrometeoroid infall onto Saturn's rings constrains their age

text: A 2024 study argued micrometeoroid impacts can vaporise rather than stain ice, so the rings may be billions of years old.
as_written: which would let clean-looking rings be billions of years old
source: Hyodo, Genda and Madeira 2024, Nature Geoscience

text: Tomkins and colleagues published in 2024 in Earth and Planetary Science Letters that Earth had a ring in the Ordovician, about 466 million years ago.
as_written: about 466 million years ago
source: Tomkins et al. 2024, Earth and Planetary Science Letters, Evidence suggesting that Earth had a ring in the Ordovician

text: The study used 21 Ordovician impact craters, all within 30 degrees of the equator when reconstructed.
as_written: They took 21 impact craters from that period
source: Tomkins et al. 2024, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

text: All 21 craters lay within 30 degrees of the paleo-equator, although most continental crust lay farther away.
as_written: All 21 lay within 30 degrees of the equator
source: Tomkins et al. 2024, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

text: The authors suggest the ring lasted for tens of millions of years and its shadow may have contributed to the Hirnantian glaciation.
as_written: may have lasted for tens of millions of years
source: Tomkins et al. 2024, Earth and Planetary Science Letters; Monash University release

text: The Hirnantian ice age occurred about 445 million years ago and was one of the coldest intervals of the last half billion years.
as_written: about 445 million years ago, one of the coldest stretches of the last half billion years
source: Palaeoclimate literature on the Late Ordovician glaciation, e.g. Finnegan et al. 2011, Science

text: Ordovician rock layers contain unusual amounts of meteorite debris from a large space break-up.
as_written: hold an unusual amount of meteorite debris
source: Schmitz et al. 2019, Science Advances, L-chondrite asteroid breakup in the Middle Ordovician
